items.title: 11.4.3 Graph of y = cos x from - 2pi to 2pi

source_refs.note: Book p. 207-209: 11.4.3 Graph of y = cos x: range lines, table x / cos x, graphs 0 to 360 and -360 to 360, properties (i)-(xi); (vii) prints minimum 1 for -1.

blocks.text: We know that the period of cosine function is \(2\pi\), so we will first draw the graph for the interval from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) (from \(0\) to \(2\pi\)).
We know the range of the cosine function is \([-1, 1]\), so the graph will be between the horizontal lines \(y = +1\) and \(y = -1\).
The table of the ordered pairs satisfying \(y = \cos x\) is as follows:

blocks.caption: Ordered pairs satisfying \(y = \cos x\), \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\) (printed across the page in the book; turned on its side here to fit a phone)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Compare this table with the sine table of 11.4.2: the same numbers appear, but shifted. \(\cos 0^{\circ} = 1\) is the value \(\sin 90^{\circ}\); \(\cos 30^{\circ} = 0.87\) is \(\sin 120^{\circ}\), and so on. In general \(\cos x = \sin(x + 90^{\circ})\), so the cosine graph is the sine graph moved \(90^{\circ}\) to the left.
The graph of \(y = \cos x\) from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) is given below:
bold: The graph of \(y = \cos x\) from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) is given below:

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cos x from 0 to 360 degrees. The x-axis is marked every 30 degrees (with pi/2, pi, 3pi/2, 2pi below), the y-axis at 1, 0.5, -0.5, -1, with dashed lines y = 1 and y = -1. The smooth wave starts at the maximum (0, 1), crosses the x-axis at 90 degrees, reaches the minimum (180, -1), crosses again at 270 degrees and returns to (360, 1).
blocks.caption: Graph of y = cos x from 0° to 360° (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Follow the same steps as for sine: scale (\(10^{\circ}\) per small square on the \(x\)-axis, 1 unit per big square on the \(y\)-axis), axes, plot the 13 points, join with one smooth curve. The cosine curve starts at its highest point \((0, 1)\), not at the origin. It is positive in Quadrants I and IV and negative in Quadrants II and III.

In the similar way, we can draw the graph for the interval from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(-360^{\circ}\). This will complete the graph of \(y = \cos x\) from \(-360^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\), i.e. from \(-2\pi\) to \(2\pi\), which is given below:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For negative angles \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\), e.g. \(\cos(-60^{\circ}) = \cos 60^{\circ} = 0.5\). So the left half of the graph is the mirror image of the right half in the \(y\)-axis.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cos x from -360 to 360 degrees (-2pi to 2pi), x-axis marked every 90 degrees with radian names, points every 30 degrees. Two complete waves between the dashed lines y = 1 and y = -1: maxima at -360, 0 and 360 degrees, minima at -180 and 180 degrees, zeros at -270, -90, 90 and 270 degrees. The graph is a mirror image about the y-axis.
blocks.caption: Graph of y = cos x from −360° to 360° (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: As in the case of sine graph, the cosine graph is also extended on both sides of \(x\)-axis through an interval of \(2\pi\).
Properties of graph of cosine function (y = cos x)

items: (i) The domain is the set of real numbers \((-\infty < x < \infty)\).
(ii) The range includes all real numbers from \(-1\) to \(1\), inclusive, \([-1, 1]\).
(iii) The graph of cosine function is continuous for all real numbers.
(iv) The period of cosine function is \(2\pi\). Mathematically, we can express it as \(\cos(\theta + 2\pi) = \cos\theta\).
(v) The cosine function is an even function, as the graph of cosine function is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis. Mathematically, it can be written as \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\).
(vi) The maximum value of \(y = \cos x\) is \(1\) when \(x = \pi n\), where \(n\) is an even integer.
(vii) The minimum value of \(y = \cos x\) is 1 when \(x = \pi n\), where \(n\) is an odd integer.
book_errors: is 1 when \(x = \pi n\), where \(n\) is an odd integer

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In property (vii) the book prints the minimum value of \(y = \cos x\) as \(1\) (the minus sign is missing). Correct: the minimum value of \(y = \cos x\) is \(-1\), when \(x = \pi n\) with \(n\) odd, e.g. \(\cos 180^{\circ} = -1\). A minimum of \(1\) is impossible, because \(1\) is the maximum (property (vi)).

items: (viii) The \(x\)-intercept of the cosine function occurs at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + \pi n\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(ix) The \(y\)-intercept of the cosine function is \(1\).
(x) The amplitude of cosine function is \(1\).
(xi) In unit circle \(\cos\theta\) is equal to the \(x\)-coordinate of the given point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check on the graph: (vi) even \(n = -2, 0, 2\) give \(-360^{\circ}, 0^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}\), the three peaks; (vii) odd \(n = -1, 1\) give \(-180^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}\), the two lowest points; (viii) \(n = -2, -1, 0, 1\) give \(-270^{\circ}, -90^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}, 270^{\circ}\), where the curve cuts the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Sine and cosine are easy to confuse in a sketch. Test one point: at \(x = 0\), \(\sin 0 = 0\) (start at the origin) but \(\cos 0 = 1\) (start at the top).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Same shape as sine, moved \(90^{\circ}\) to the left: \(\cos x = \sin(x + 90^{\circ})\).
2. Range \([-1, 1]\), period \(2\pi\), amplitude \(1\), continuous everywhere.
3. Peaks at even multiples of \(\pi\), lowest points (\(-1\)) at odd multiples of \(\pi\).
4. Zeros at \(\frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\); \(y\)-intercept \(1\).
5. Even function: the graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Copying the misprint: the minimum of \(\cos x\) is \(-1\), not \(1\).
2. Putting the zeros of cosine at \(0, \pi, 2\pi\): those are the zeros of sine. Cosine is zero at \(90^{\circ}\) and \(270^{\circ}\).
3. Drawing the left half as an upside-down copy: for cosine the left half is a mirror image, because \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\).
